content.text: Welcome to The Studio. You finished your Launch Plan, which means you've already done the thinking most people skip. In the Tutorials you decided
what
your business is. Here you set up
how
it runs: the email, the payments, the pages and the tools that let you take your first customer.
How The Studio works
There are two parts.
Start Here
is five short lessons everyone does, because every business needs them whatever the path: a business email and safe logins, a way to get paid, a money tracker and a simple look. Then you open
your track
, the one that matches the lead path in your Launch Plan:
Track 1: Social Selling and Influence
Track 2: Affiliate and Reselling
Track 3: The Small Hobby Business
Track 4: Building Something Bigger

Every lesson ends with something actually set up, not just written down. Most take 20 to 45 minutes. One or two a week is a good pace. You're welcome to peek at the other tracks too, since paths often mix.
Keep your Launch Plan beside you
It's your map. Every lesson tells you who can skip it, so you only set up what your plan needs.
Our two rules
Free first, pay when it pays.
Start on the free plan. Upgrade only when the business is earning enough to cover it, or when the free version is costing you time or sales.
Only set up what your Launch Plan needs.
A shiny tool you don't use is just another monthly charge.
How we recommend tools

We use many of these tools in our own business. Our Tool Shelf, pinned at the top of The Studio, lists every tool we mention, with the free option first. Some of the links on it earn SWC a commission if you sign up, at no extra cost to you. We'll always tell you when that's the case, and we never recommend a tool because it pays us. If a free tool does the job, we'll say so. Before you pay for anything, post it in the
Ask Before You Buy
thread and we'll give you an honest second opinion.
Staying safe
The moment you look like a business online, the scammers notice. Watch for:
Messages offering to "grow your page" or "get you 1,000 followers" for a fee
Warnings that your account will be shut down unless you click a link
A customer who "accidentally" overpays and asks you to send back the difference
Anyone asking for a password or a code sent to your phone

Three habits keep you safe. Never click a link in a message you weren't expecting; go to the website yourself instead. Never share a password or a code, with anyone. No one from SWC, your bank or any platform will ever ask for one. And if a message is urgent and about money, slow down. Real problems can wait an hour while you check.
Help is close by
If you get stuck, post in the
Show Your Setup
thread, ask Clara, or bring it to our monthly live
Studio Desk
session, where we work through setups together on screen.

Before you open a single business account, set up the home base everything else will hang from. It keeps your business separate from your personal life, makes you look professional from day one, and protects you if a password ever leaks. It takes about 30 minutes.
Step 1: A business email

Every tool in The Studio asks for an email address, so use the same business one for all of them. A free Gmail address is perfectly fine to start, for example carolsquilts@gmail.com or carol.paperworkplanning@gmail.com. Keep it short, easy to say out loud, and close to your business name.
Later, once you have your own website name (a domain), you can get an address like carol@carolsquilts.ca. Track 4 covers that. Don't let it hold you up now.
Step 2: A password manager
A password manager remembers every password for you and creates strong ones you'd never guess. You only remember one: your master password. We suggest
Bitwarden
, which is free, or the one already built into your phone or browser (Apple Passwords or Google Password Manager).
Choose a master password made of four or five unrelated words, such as "teapot river violet seventy". Write it on paper and keep it somewhere safe at home, not on your computer.
Step 3: Turn on 2-step login
With 2-step login (also called two-factor authentication), signing in needs your password
and

a code from your phone. Even if someone steals your password, they can't get in. Turn it on for your business email first, then for every new account you open in The Studio. When a site gives you backup codes, save them in your password manager.
Step 4: One folder for everything
Your Gmail address comes with free Google Drive storage. Make one folder called "My Business" with these folders inside:
Money
Receipts
Brand (logo, colours, photos)
Customers
Admin (registrations, licences, insurance)
Worksheets
When you download something for your business, it goes here. Nothing gets lost in your downloads folder again.
Example (not a real member):

Joan set up joan.gardencoach@gmail.com, installed Bitwarden on her phone and laptop, and turned on 2-step login. Two months later she got an email saying her Facebook password had been changed. Because her business email had 2-step login, she reset everything in ten minutes and lost nothing.
Your action step:
Create your business email, set up a password manager, turn on 2-step login for your email, and make your "My Business" folder.

The first time someone pays you for your work is a moment you'll remember. Let's make sure it's easy for them and safe for you. You only need
one
way to get paid to start. You can add more later.
Your options (Canadian fees, October 2026)
Interac e-Transfer
Best for: Local clients, friends of friends, small numbers of sales
What it costs you: Free with many bank accounts; some banks charge a small fee
Square
Best for: Markets, classes, in-person sales, invoices
What it costs you: 2.5% per credit card tapped in person; 0.75% + 7¢ for debit in person; 2.8% + 30¢ online or by invoice
Stripe
Best for: Selling online, bookings, subscriptions
What it costs you: 2.9% + 30¢ per Canadian card; no monthly fee
PayPal
Best for: Customers who prefer PayPal
What it costs you: 2.9% + 30¢ per Canadian payment
None of these charge a monthly fee for the basic service. You pay a small amount each time you're paid. If you live in the US, the fees are similar; check each company's website for your country.
Which one fits your path?
Social selling and services:
start with e-Transfer for your first few clients, then Stripe once you take bookings online (many booking and course tools, such as Systeme.io and Skool, use Stripe behind the scenes).
Affiliate and reselling:
affiliate programs pay
you
, usually by PayPal or direct deposit, so set up PayPal and have your business bank details ready. For resale, the marketplace handles payment.
Hobby business:
Square, because it works at a market table and online.
Building something bigger:
Stripe, because nearly every website and course tool connects to it.
Fees are a cost of doing business

Build them into your price, as you did in Lesson 9. On a $50 sale paid online through Square, the fee is $1.40 plus 30¢, so you keep $48.30. It's small, but over a year it adds up, and it belongs in your money tracker (next lesson).
Connect it to your business bank account
In Lesson 12 you opened (or booked a time to open) a separate account for your business. Send all your payouts there, not to your personal account. It makes tax time far easier.
Test it with $1

Ask a friend to pay you $1 using your new option, then refund it. Now you know exactly what your customer sees, how long the money takes to arrive, and how to give a refund. Much better to learn that with a friend than with your first customer.
A scam to know about.

Someone "accidentally" pays you too much and asks you to send the difference back by e-Transfer or gift card. The original payment later bounces and your money is gone. Only ever refund through the same tool the money came in on, and only after it has fully arrived.
Your action step:
Choose your payment option, connect it to your business bank account, and do your $1 test and refund.

You don't need to love bookkeeping. You need a simple habit: write down every dollar that comes in and goes out, and look at it once a month. That's what tells you whether your business is really working, and it makes tax time calm instead of frantic.
This is general information to help you get organized, not tax advice. Your accountant is the right person for questions about your own situation.
Choose your tracker
Our spreadsheet template (free).
Download it from Resources & Tools. Best if you have fewer than about 20 sales and expenses a month.
Wave (free Starter plan).

Made for small Canadian and US businesses. It handles invoices, income and expenses, and simple reports. The free plan means typing in each transaction; the paid Pro plan adds automatic bank imports and receipt scanning.
QuickBooks (paid).
Worth it once you work with a bookkeeper or accountant who uses it, or your business is getting busy.
Start with the template or Wave. You can always move later.
What to record for every transaction

The date, what it was, money in or money out, the amount, a category, and whether you've saved the receipt. If you're registered for GST/HST (Canada) or sales tax (US), also record the tax you collected.
Keep your categories simple
Sales
Payment and platform fees
Supplies and materials
Software and subscriptions
Advertising
Phone and internet (the business share)
Training
Travel and mileage
Set aside your tax money every time

In Lesson 12 you chose a percentage to put aside for tax. Each time money comes in, move that percentage to a separate savings account straight away. Then the money is there when you need it, and nothing comes as a shock.
Your monthly money date
Pick one day near the start of each month and give it 20 minutes, ideally with a cup of something nice:
Enter anything you missed, and check it against your bank statement.
Make sure every receipt is saved in your Receipts folder.
Move any tax set-aside you forgot.
Look at the bottom line: money in, minus money out. Is it going the right way?
Look at your subscriptions. Cancel anything you didn't use last month.
Example (not a real member):

Marion sells hand-dyed yarn. At her third money date she noticed her payment fees and a design app she'd forgotten about were costing $38 a month. She cancelled the $15 app and raised her prices by $1 a skein. She sells about 50 skeins a month, so her monthly profit went up by about $65.
Your action step:
Choose your tracker, set up your categories, enter anything from this month, and put your money date in your calendar as a repeating event.

You don't need an expensive designer to look professional. You need to look
consistent

: the same colours, the same fonts and the same face everywhere people meet you. Consistency is what makes people recognize you and trust you. Today you'll make a one-page brand sheet in Canva that you'll use for everything that follows.
Step 1: Three feeling words
How do you want people to feel when they meet your business? Calm, cheerful, cozy, confident, elegant, earthy? Pick three. Every choice below should fit them.
Step 2: Two or three colours

One main colour, one accent and one neutral (cream, grey or soft white) is plenty. An easy way to find them: upload a photo you love to Canva's free colour palette tool and it pulls out the colours for you. Write down each colour's code, the six characters after the # sign, such as #A8616B. That's how you'll match it everywhere.
Step 3: Two fonts
One for headings, which can have some personality, and one for reading, which must be easy on the eyes. Avoid fancy script for anything people need to read, especially on a phone screen.
Step 4: A simple logo
Your business name typed in your heading font, in your main colour, is a perfectly good logo. Add a small symbol if you like. Canva has logo templates you can change to suit you.

One caution: Canva's terms don't let you trademark a design built from its templates or stock graphics. If you think you'll want to trademark your logo one day, keep it to your name in a font, or have a designer make it.
Step 5: A profile photo

People buy from people. Use one clear, warm photo of you, the same one everywhere. Stand facing a window in daylight, have a friend hold the phone at your eye level, frame from the shoulders up against a plain background, and smile like you're greeting a customer. Take twenty and pick the best.
Step 6: Put it on one page

In Canva, make a one-page brand sheet with your three feeling words, your colours and their codes, your two fonts, your logo and your photo. Save it to your Brand folder. Whenever you make anything, open this first.
Example (not a real member):

Beth runs paperwork planning sessions for families caring for ageing parents. Her words were calm, organized and kind. She chose a soft navy, a warm gold and cream, a clean heading font and an easy reading font. Her logo is "Beth Ross Planning" in navy with a small gold house. It took her one afternoon.
Your action step:
Make your brand sheet in Canva and save it to your Brand folder. Then update your profile photo wherever you already have a business account.

The fastest way to burn out online is trying to be everywhere. The women who do well with social selling pick
one
platform, show up there consistently for a few months, and only add a second once the first is working. Today you choose yours.
Go where your "who" already is
Look at the sentence from your Idea Test (Lesson 19): "I help [who] with [what]..." Then think about where those people spend time online, not where you feel you
should
be.
Facebook:
strongest for women over 45, local communities and groups. Great for services, local businesses and community building.
Instagram:
visual and lifestyle topics: home, food, style, crafts, wellness. Short videos (Reels) reach new people.
YouTube:
teaching and how-to. Slower to grow, but videos keep being found for years.
Pinterest:
people planning and searching (recipes, gardens, crafts, gifts). It sends people to links, which makes it great alongside affiliate links or a shop.
LinkedIn:
professional services, consulting, coaching for working people.
Three questions to decide
Where did the five people from your Idea Test say they spend time online?
Which platform do you already use and feel comfortable on?
Which suits how you like to share: writing, photos, talking on video, or teaching?
If two platforms tie, pick the one you already use. Comfort beats strategy when you're starting out.
Facebook groups count

You don't need a big following on Facebook to sell. Joining three or four groups where your people already gather, and being genuinely helpful there, often brings first clients faster than posting on your own page. (Follow each group's rules about promotion.)
Example (not a real member):

Carol helps women caring for ageing parents get organized. She tried Instagram first because everyone said to. But the women she talked to in her Idea Test were in Facebook caregiver groups. She switched to Facebook, answered questions in two groups for a month, and booked her first three planning sessions from there.
Your action step:
Answer the three questions, choose your one platform, and write down three Facebook groups or accounts where your people already gather.

t1.name: A Profile That Says What You Do

content.text: When someone lands on your profile, they decide in a few seconds whether you're for them. Your profile has one job: tell the right person what you do, who it's for, and what to do next.
Your name and photo
Use your real name, or your name plus a few words: "Carol Hughes | Caregiver Paperwork Help". Use the profile photo from your brand sheet (Lesson S5), the same one everywhere.
Your bio, in three lines
Who you help and how:
your sentence from Lesson 19. "I help women caring for ageing parents get the paperwork sorted."
Why you:
one line of proof from your own life. "Former office manager. Did it for my own mum."
What to do next:
"Book a free 15-minute chat below" or "Get my free checklist below."
Plain and clear beats clever. If a stranger can't say what you do after reading it, rewrite it.
One link that leads somewhere
Most platforms give you one clickable link. Make it count:
Linktree (free):
a simple page with several buttons, for example "Book a session", "Free checklist" and "Shop". Good to start.
Stan Store ($29/month):
a link page that also sells, so people can book, pay or download right there. Worth it once you have something to sell, not before.
Your own website:
if you already have one, link straight to your offer or sign-up page.
For now, your link can go to your sign-up page (Lesson A4) or your booking page (Lesson A5). You'll come back and update it.
Pin your best post
Most platforms let you pin a post to the top of your profile. Pin one that introduces you: who you are, who you help, and a little of your story.
Example (not a real member):

Carol's old Facebook bio said "Mum, gardener, retired." Her new one says: "I help women caring for ageing parents get the paperwork sorted. 30 years running a busy office, and I did it all for my own mum. Book a free 15-minute chat below."
Your action step:

Social selling runs on showing up regularly, not on going viral. Three posts a week, every week, beats a burst of twenty followed by silence. Today you'll set up a routine that takes about an hour a week.
Step 1: Your three topics
Pick three things you'll always talk about. Everything you post fits one of them. For Carol:
Help:
practical tips ("the five documents to find before a hospital visit")
Story:
her own experience with her mum, and lessons learned
Offer:
what she does, client wins (with permission), how to book
Most of your posts should help or tell a story. About one in five can be about your offer.
Step 2: Ten post ideas
Write ten ideas now, across your three topics. Use the questions people asked you in your Idea Test. Every question someone asks is a post.
Step 3: Make them look like you
In Canva, make two or three post templates in your brand colours and fonts (from your brand sheet). Next time, you just change the words.
Step 4: Video, if you're willing

Short videos reach the most new people on most platforms. You don't need fancy gear: your phone, a window and something to say. CapCut (free) adds captions automatically, which matters because many people watch with the sound off.
If you record longer videos, such as a live session or a talk,
OpusClip
can cut one long video into several short clips for you. It has a free plan to try.
Step 5: Batch and schedule
Pick one hour a week. Write and design that week's three posts, then schedule them.
Meta Business Suite
is free and schedules posts to Facebook and Instagram. Most other platforms have their own scheduler.
Step 6: Talk back
Social selling is
social
. Spend ten minutes a day replying to comments and commenting kindly on other people's posts in your groups. That's where relationships, and clients, come from.
Your action step:
Choose your three topics, write ten post ideas, make two Canva templates, and schedule your first week of posts.

Your followers belong to the platform. If it changes its rules, or your account is hacked, they can vanish overnight. Your email list belongs to you. It's also where most sales actually happen, because an email arrives in someone's inbox instead of scrolling past. Today you'll set up a simple list with a gift that makes people want to join.
Step 1: Your sign-up gift
Offer something small and useful in exchange for an email address. It should solve one small problem for your "who":
A one-page checklist ("The 10 Papers to Find Before a Crisis")
A short guide or recipe card
A 10-minute video
A quiz that tells them something about themselves
Make it in Canva using your brand sheet, and save it as a PDF.
Step 2: Choose your email tool
MailerLite (our pick to start):

free for up to 500 subscribers and 12,000 emails a month, with sign-up forms, simple automations and landing pages. The free plan shows a small MailerLite logo at the bottom of your emails. We use MailerLite ourselves.
Kit:
also has a free plan and is popular with creators.
ScoreApp:
if you'd love a quiz as your gift. It's a paid tool, so save it for later unless a quiz is central to your business.
Step 3: Your sign-up page
In MailerLite, make a landing page: a headline that names the problem, two or three lines about the gift, your photo, and a sign-up box. Put the link to this page in your profile (Lesson A2).
Step 4: Your welcome email

Set up an automation so that everyone who signs up gets an email straight away with their gift, a warm hello, a little about you, and one question: "What made you sign up?" The replies tell you exactly what your people need.
The rules for emailing people

Canada's anti-spam law (CASL) and the US CAN-SPAM Act both apply to business email. In short: only email people who signed up or clearly agreed, say who you are, include a mailing address, and include an unsubscribe link. MailerLite adds the unsubscribe link for you. You can use a P.O. box instead of your home address. Never add people to your list just because you have their email.
Example (not a real member):

Carol's gift is "The 10 Papers to Find Before a Crisis", a one-page checklist. She shares it in her Facebook groups when people ask for help. In her first month, 64 people joined her list, and two booked a session from her welcome email.
Your action step:
Make your gift, set up MailerLite (or Kit), build your sign-up page, write your welcome email, and sign up yourself to test it.

t1.name: Your First Offer, Ready to Book or Buy

content.text: You tested your offer with real people in Lesson 19. Now make it easy to say yes: one link where someone can understand the offer, pay and book, without a single back-and-forth email.
Step 1: Write your offer card
Six lines, kept somewhere you can copy from:
Name of the offer ("Paperwork Planning Session")
Who it's for
What they get ("a 60-minute video call and a personalized checklist emailed afterwards")
The result ("you'll know exactly what's missing and what to do first")
The price
How to book or buy
Step 2: Choose your setup.
Pick the one that matches what you sell.
If you sell sessions or services: payment link plus booking link
Stripe Payment Links
are free to create in your Stripe account. You get one link for your offer at your price.
Calendly's free plan

gives you one type of booking with your available times. It can't take payment on the free plan, so send the booking link in the "thank you" message after payment, or upgrade to a paid Calendly plan later to take payment at booking.
For the call itself:
Zoom's free plan limits meetings to 40 minutes, so use Google Meet (free with your Gmail) or upgrade Zoom if your sessions run longer.
If you sell something to download (a guide, a recording, templates)
Payhip:
free to start; it keeps 5% of each sale plus card fees, and delivers the file automatically.
Stan Store ($29/month):
worth it if you're already using it as your link page.
If you'd like everything in one place: Systeme.io

It has a free plan that includes a sales page, checkout, email list and even a simple course, all under one login. We use it ourselves. It takes a little longer to learn, but you'll have fewer tools to juggle.
Step 3: A simple sales post or page

Turn your offer card into a post you can pin, or a short page: the problem, what they get, what changes for them, a few words about you, the price and the button. Use the words your Idea Test people used.
Step 4: Test the whole journey
Ask a friend to go through it all: click, pay (you'll refund them), book, and get the confirmation. Fix anything that confused her.
Example (not a real member):

Carol created a Stripe payment link for her $95 Paperwork Planning Session. The thank-you message after payment says "Now pick your time" with her Calendly link. She pinned a Facebook post with her offer card and the payment link, and added the same link to her Linktree.
Your action step:
Write your offer card, set up your payment and booking (or your download), put the link in your profile, and test the whole journey with a friend.

Once people trust you, they'll want to know what you use, read and recommend. That's a second way to earn: affiliate links and, later, partnerships with brands. Done honestly, it's a service to your followers. Done carelessly, it costs you their trust. Today you'll set it up the honest way.
Step 1: List what you already recommend

Write down ten products, books or tools you genuinely use and would tell a friend about. For Carol: a document organizer binder, a password manager, a book on caring for parents, a label maker. Your best affiliate links will come from this list, not from whatever pays the most.
Step 2: Join two or three programs
Amazon Associates

(Canada or US): covers almost anything sold on Amazon. Commissions are usually small, between 1% and 10% depending on the category, and you need three sales within 180 days of approval to keep your account.
The company's own program:
scroll to the bottom of a brand's website and look for "Affiliates" or "Partners". Many run through networks such as Impact or Awin.
Tools you use for your business:
software companies often pay more, sometimes 20% to 30% every month the person stays.
Track 2 goes much deeper if affiliate income becomes a bigger part of your plan.
Step 3: Your disclosure line
In Canada, Ad Standards' guidelines say to disclose an affiliate link or any paid relationship on
every
post, before the link, in plain words. In the US, the FTC says the same. A note in your bio isn't enough. Pick your line now and use it every time:
"I earn a small commission if you buy through this link, at no extra cost to you."
Or short, at the start of a caption: #AffiliateLink or #CommissionEarned
For videos, say it out loud near the start, not just in the caption.
Step 4: Saying yes (or no) to brands

As you grow, brands may offer free products or payment for a post. Before you say yes, ask: would I recommend this without being paid? Does it fit my people? Free products count as a paid relationship, so they need the same disclosure.
Example (not a real member):

Carol wrote a post called "The 5 things in my caregiving binder", with an Amazon link for each and her disclosure line at the top. It's now her most-saved post, and it earns a few dollars every month without her lifting a finger.
Your action step:

Affiliate income is often sold as "passive income while you sleep." It can be, eventually, but only after you've built trust and a body of helpful content. Before you set anything up, let's look at how the money really works, so your expectations match reality.
The basic idea
A company gives you a special link. When someone clicks it and buys, the company pays you a share of the sale, called a commission. The customer pays the same price either way.
Four things decide what you earn
The commission rate.
Physical products usually pay 1% to 10%. Software and online services often pay 20% to 50%, and some keep paying every month the customer stays.
The tracking window.
Your link only counts for a set time after someone clicks. On Amazon it's 24 hours (longer if they add to cart). Some software programs track for 60 or 90 days.
How many people see your link.
A great link nobody sees earns nothing. That's why content (Lesson B4) matters more than which program you join.
How much they trust you.
People buy what a trusted friend recommends. Honest reviews, including what you
don't
like, earn more over time than hype.
What the numbers look like

If you recommend a $40 kitchen tool on Amazon at a 4% commission, you earn $1.60 per sale. Twenty sales a month is $32. A $20-a-month software tool at 30% recurring earns you $6 a month per person who signs up, for as long as they stay. Fifteen people is $90 a month, every month. Both are real; they just grow differently.
Reselling is different

Reselling means buying items (thrift finds, vintage, clearance) and selling them for more. You hold stock, take photos and ship, so it's more hands-on, but money arrives faster and you control the price. Many women do both. Lesson B5 covers reselling.

What they'll ask for

Most programs want to see where you'll share links: a website, blog, Pinterest, YouTube, Instagram or Facebook page. Have your profile set up with a few helpful posts first (Lesson B3 and B4). If you're turned down, build some content and apply again in a month or two. It's common and not personal.

US companies ask Canadians to complete a W-8BEN tax form, which confirms you're not a US taxpayer. It's a short online form. Affiliate income is business income, so it goes in your money tracker (Lesson S4).
Read the rules before you post

Every program has rules about where you can share links. Common ones: no links in private emails (Amazon is strict about this), no paying for ads on the brand's name, and always disclose. Breaking the rules can mean losing all your earnings.

content.text: Your recommendations need a home people can come back to: one place that holds your favourites, so a link shared once keeps earning for months. Today you'll set it up, along with the disclosure that keeps you honest and inside the rules.
Choose your home (pick one to start)
A link page (Linktree, free):
the simplest. A page of buttons such as "My garden tools", "Seed-starting kit" and "Books I love". Put it in your social profile.
A Pinterest board or two:
Pinterest is where people go to plan and shop, and pins keep being found for months or years. Each pin can carry an affiliate link (follow each program's rules about Pinterest).
A simple website or blog:
more work, but the strongest long-term home, because people find blog posts through Google. Wix and Systeme.io both have free plans. Track 4 covers websites if you want to go further.
Whichever you choose, organize it the way your people think: "for beginners", "under $25", "gifts for gardeners".
Your disclosures

This isn't optional. In Canada, Ad Standards' guidelines say to disclose any affiliate link or paid relationship clearly, on every post or page, before the link. In the US, the FTC says the same. Your followers deserve to know, and most of them won't mind at all.
On your link page, website or Pinterest profile:
a clear line near the top, such as "Some links on this page are affiliate links. If you buy through them, I earn a small commission at no extra cost to you. I only recommend things I use."
If you're an Amazon Associate:
Amazon requires this exact sentence wherever you use its links: "As an Amazon Associate I earn from qualifying purchases."
On every social post or pin with a link:
at the start, not buried at the end: "#AffiliateLink" or "Commission earned if you buy."
In videos:
say it out loud near the start, and put it on screen.

Nobody wants to be sold to. Everyone wants help choosing. The best affiliate content answers a real question someone is asking, and the link is simply the easiest next step. Today you'll make three pieces that work for months.
Three kinds of content that earn
The honest review.
One product you really use. What it does, who it's for, what you love and what annoys you. Admitting the downsides is what makes people believe the upsides. Include your own photos if you can.
The "what I'd buy" list.
"5 tools I'd buy again if I started gardening tomorrow." Short reasons for each. People save and share lists.
The seasonal gift guide.
"Gifts for the gardener who has everything, under $30." Gift guides earn most in November and December, so make them in October.
Where to share them
Pinterest:
make a pin for each piece (Canva has pin templates) linking to your link page or blog.
Facebook groups:
where allowed, answer people's questions with your honest experience. Check each group's rules about links; often it's better to help in the comments and let people ask for your link.
Your own page or profile:
post each piece, pin your best one, and point back to your link page.
Your email list:
if you have one, send your list or gift guide to subscribers. (Check your program's rules; Amazon doesn't allow its links in emails, so link to your blog or page instead.)
Make it yours

Your age and experience are an advantage here. "I've been gardening for 40 years, and this is the only kneeler that hasn't fallen apart" is more convincing than any ad. Write the way you'd talk to a friend over the fence.
Use AI as a helper, not a writer

AI tools can help you outline a list or tidy your words (see the bonus lesson, AI as Your Assistant). But the experience, opinions and photos must be yours. That's what people trust, and copied AI reviews are easy to spot.

If you have an eye for a good find, reselling can bring in money within weeks. It's the most hands-on part of this track: you buy, photograph, list, pack and ship. Today you'll set up a routine and list your first five items. Skip this lesson if you're doing affiliate only.
Step 1: Choose where you'll sell
Start with one or two places that suit what you sell:
Facebook Marketplace:
free for local pickup. Best for furniture, household items and anything heavy.
Poshmark:
clothing, shoes and accessories. It keeps a share of each sale (around 20% on most items), and you ship using its prepaid label.
eBay:
almost anything, especially collectibles, vintage and items people search for by name. Fees are a percentage of the sale and vary by category.
Etsy:
for vintage items, which Etsy defines as at least 20 years old.
Step 2: Source smart
Start with your own closets and cupboards; you get to learn with zero risk. Then thrift stores, garage sales and estate sales. Before you buy anything, look up
sold
listings (not asking prices) on eBay or Poshmark on your phone to see what it actually sells for. A good rule of thumb: buy only if it sells for at least three times what you'd pay.
Step 3: List it well
Photos in daylight on a plain background, from several angles, plus any flaws (see the bonus lesson, Photos That Sell).
A title with the words a buyer would search: brand, item, size, colour.
Honest condition notes. Flaws you mention up front don't become returns.
Price from sold listings, allowing for fees and shipping.
Step 4: Ship without stress

In Canada, Canada Post's free Solutions for Small Business program gives you discounted rates, and you can buy and print labels online with Snap Ship. Keep a small packing kit: mailers, boxes, tape, a kitchen scale and a measuring tape. Weigh and measure items
before
you list them so your shipping price is right.
Step 5: Stay safe with local sales
Meet in a public place in daylight; many police stations have marked exchange zones. Take payment by e-Transfer before handing over the item, or cash in hand. Bring a friend for anything large.
Keep records
Resale income is business income. Record what you paid for each item and what it sold for in your tracker (Lesson B6), and keep your receipts.

You make something lovely. Now, where will people find it and buy it? There are four main ways to sell a hobby. Most women start with one or two and add more once those are running smoothly.
1. Markets and craft fairs

Farmers' markets, Christmas craft fairs, church bazaars and pop-ups. You pay a table fee, meet buyers face to face and hear what they think. Great for learning what sells. Popular fairs fill up months ahead, and some are juried (they choose who gets in), so apply early.
2. Online
Etsy:
buyers are already there looking for handmade and vintage. Small fees on every listing and sale.
Your own online shop:
Square Online has a free plan; Shopify suits a bigger range of products. No marketplace to bring you buyers, so you bring them yourself.
3. Local shops
Gift shops, cafes, garden centres and galleries often carry local makers.
Consignment:
the shop displays your work and pays you when it sells, often around 60% to you and 40% to them. Low risk, slower money.
Wholesale:
the shop buys your work outright, usually at about half your retail price. You need your prices high enough to allow for that.
4. Teaching your skill
Workshops and classes, in person or online. Often the best money per hour for a maker, and it brings in new customers for your products. Lesson C4 covers it.
How to choose
Look at your Launch Plan: your hours, your comfort number and your Idea Test results.
Want to meet people and get feedback fast? Start with markets.
Prefer working from home, or live far from town? Start with Etsy.
Have a few products that sell steadily? Approach local shops.
Love explaining how you do it? Add a class.
Check the rules first

In Lesson 12 you checked whether you need a business licence. Some products have extra rules: food, cosmetics and soaps, candles and children's items often have safety or labelling requirements. A quick call to your city or health authority before you sell saves trouble later.

Gwen makes quilted table runners. She chose two ways to start: a Christmas craft fair in November and a beginners' quilting class at her community centre. The fair showed her which colours sold out; the class filled with women who then bought her runners.

An online shop works for you while you're making, sleeping or at the market. Today you'll open one with five listings. If you're only selling at markets for now, you can skip this lesson and come back later.
Choose your shop

Best for: Selling to people who already know you; works with your Square reader
Monthly cost: Free plan available

If you already use Square at markets (Lesson C3), Square Online keeps your stock and sales in one place. If you want strangers to find you, Etsy brings the buyers. Shopify suits a larger range once you're growing.
Step 1: Shop basics

Use your business email (Lesson S2), your logo and colours (Lesson S5), and connect payouts to your business bank account. Write a short "About" section: who you are, how you make things, and why. Buyers of handmade love the story.
Step 2: Photos

Photos sell handmade. Daylight, a plain background, several angles, one close-up of the detail, and one showing size (in a hand, on a table). The bonus lesson, Photos That Sell, walks you through it with just your phone.
Step 3: Titles and descriptions
Title: the words a buyer would type into search. "Quilted Christmas Table Runner, Red and Green, Handmade, 14 x 48 inches" beats "Holly Joy."
Description, in this order: what it is and who it's for; size, materials and care; how it's made; shipping or pickup. An AI tool can help you tidy the words, as long as every fact comes from you.
Step 4: Shipping or pickup

Weigh and measure each item packed, then set shipping prices using Canada Post's rates (its free Solutions for Small Business program gives discounts). Offer local pickup if you're happy to. Write down how long you need to make or ship each order, and say so in the listing.
Step 5: Five listings, then open

Fewer people carry cash every year. A maker who can only take cash at a market loses sales she never even hears about. Today you'll set up card payments on your phone and pack a market kit, so every market day starts calm.
Step 1: Take cards on your phone

Set it up before market day:
Add each product to Square's item list with its price. Then every sale is recorded by item, and you'll know exactly what sold.

Also put up a small sign with your business email for e-Transfers, and bring a cash float for people who still pay cash.
Step 2: Your table
Height:
raise some items up with crates or stands. Things at eye level sell; things flat on the table get missed.
Prices on everything:
many people won't ask. Clear price tags sell more.
Your name:
a sign or banner with your business name and logo (Lesson S5), so people remember you.
A way to find you later:
cards with your shop link, and a QR code that goes to your email sign-up page, so people who don't buy today can buy later. (Only add people who sign up themselves.)
Step 3: Pack the kit
Keep it all in one bin so you're never hunting the night before:
Phone, card reader and a charged power bank
Cash float in small bills and coins, in a pouch you keep on you
Price tags, pens, tape, scissors and clips
Table cover, stands, signs and business cards
Bags or wrapping
Water, a snack, a warm layer and a folding chair
Your market fee receipt and any licence you need
Step 4: After the market

That evening, check Square to see what sold, note what people asked for, and record the day in your money tracker (including the table fee). Over a season, this tells you which markets are worth repeating.

The skill you've built over decades is worth money on its own, not only in the things you make. A two-hour class for eight people can earn more than a week of making, and your students often become your best customers. Today you'll plan and list your first workshop. Skip this lesson if teaching isn't for you, or come back to it later.
Step 1: Choose a beginner class

The easiest class to fill is one where people leave with something finished: "Make Your First Quilted Coaster", "Sourdough for Beginners", "Paint a Watercolour Card". Two to three hours is plenty. Keep it to one clear result.
Step 2: Where to hold it
Community centres and libraries:
many run programs and will either rent you a room or share the fees with you. Ask their program coordinator.
Local shops:
yarn, fabric, art and garden shops often host classes because students buy supplies there.
Your home:
only if you're comfortable, have the space, and have checked your insurance (Lesson 12).
Online:
a live class on Zoom or Google Meet, with a supply list sent ahead. Zoom's free plan stops at 40 minutes, so upgrade for that month or use another tool.
Step 3: Price it

Add up: materials per person, room cost, booking fees, and your time (including prep and clean-up) at the hourly rate from your Launch Plan. Divide by the number of students you can comfortably teach, then check the price against similar local classes. Set a minimum number of students, and a date to cancel by if you don't reach it.
Step 4: Take bookings
Eventbrite:
free to use for free events; for paid events it adds a fee per ticket, which you can choose to pass on to the buyer. People can find your class there too.
Square:
if you already use it, you can sell class spots as an item in your Square Online shop.
The venue's own system:
community centres often handle registration for you.
Write a clear listing: what they'll make, who it's for ("complete beginners welcome"), what's included, what to bring, date, time, place and your cancellation policy.
Step 5: Spread the word
Your email list, your social page, local Facebook groups, and the venue. Hand out cards at the end of class for your shop and your next class.

Gwen's "First Quilted Coaster" class runs at her community centre for $55, materials included. Eight women signed up, and three bought table runners afterwards. She now runs it every second month.

Many makers sell for years without knowing whether they're earning or quietly paying to have a hobby. A sale feels like income, but once you take out materials, fees and your time, the picture can change. Today you'll work out the true profit on each product, and set up a simple stock count.
Step 1: The true cost of one item
For each product, add up:
Materials:
everything that goes into it, including thread, glue and the label
Packaging:
bag, box, tissue, tag
Selling fees:
the percentage your shop, Square or the market takes
Your time:
hours to make it, at the hourly rate from your Launch Plan
A worked example
Gwen sells a table runner on Etsy for $85.
Fabric, batting and thread: $18.00
Packaging: $2.00
Etsy fees (about 11% of the sale, plus the listing fee): $9.65
Left for her time: $55.35

Each runner takes her three hours, so she's earning about $18.45 an hour. Her Launch Plan goal was $25 an hour. She has three choices: raise the price, make runners in batches so each takes less time, or buy fabric in bulk. She did all three, a little of each.
Step 2: Know your winners

Work out the hourly earnings for each product. You'll usually find one or two that earn far more for your time. Make more of those. Products that barely earn anything can stay if they bring people to your table, but you should know which ones they are.
Step 3: Count your stock

Keep a simple list of how many of each item you have ready to sell, and update it after each market and each online sale. For each product, set a "make more" number: when you get down to it, make another batch. (If you use Square for both your market and your online shop, it can count stock for you.)
Do the same for your key materials, so you're never caught out the week before a big fair.

Your best customers probably live within a short drive of you. They just don't know you exist yet. Today you'll set up three free ways for local people to find you, and a way to stay in touch with everyone who's already bought.
1. Google Business Profile (free)
When someone searches "handmade quilts near me" or "pottery class White Rock", Google shows local businesses with a profile. Setting one up is free.
Choose your business category and add your service area. If you work from home, you can
hide your address
and show only the area you serve.
Add your logo, your profile photo and at least ten photos of your work.
Add your shop link, your phone or email, and your hours or "by appointment."
Ask happy customers for a Google review. Reviews are one of the biggest reasons people choose a local business. Just ask; don't offer a discount in exchange.
2. One social page

A Facebook page or Instagram account where local people can see your work and your upcoming markets and classes. Post your market dates every week, a photo of something new, and a little of your making process. Share posts into local Facebook groups where the group rules allow it. Track 1, Lesson A3, has a simple weekly routine if you'd like one.
3. Your list of buyers
The people who've already bought from you are the most likely to buy again, and to bring friends. Give them an easy way to hear from you:
A QR code on your market table and a card in every order, going to your email sign-up page (MailerLite's free plan is plenty; see Track 1, Lesson A4)
A short email before each market, class or new collection
Only add people who sign up themselves. Canada's anti-spam law requires their consent.
4. Word of mouth, on purpose

Tell people what you do. Leave cards at the library board, the community centre and the shops that carry local makers. Offer to do a demonstration at a garden club, a church group or a seniors' centre. Women in their 60s know a lot of people, and they talk.
Example (not a real member):
Gwen set up her Google Business Profile with her area, her photos and her class schedule. Within two months, it was where most of her new class students said they'd found her.
Your action step:

You're building something with a name people will remember and search for. Before you put that name on a website, cards and social accounts, make sure it's available and that you can own it. Changing a name later is expensive and confusing. This lesson takes a few hours over a week, and it's worth getting right.
Step 1: Shortlist three names

A good business name is easy to say, easy to spell when heard, and hints at what you do or who you help. Your own name plus a description ("Diane Moore Career Coaching") is always a safe choice and grows with you. Avoid names that lock you into one product or one town if you might expand.
Step 2: Check each name
Business registry:
search your province's or state's business name registry. In most places, if you trade under a name other than your own legal name, you need to register it (Lesson 12).
Trademarks:
search the Canadian Intellectual Property Office's trademark database (or the US Patent and Trademark Office's) for the same or a very similar name in your field.
Google:
search it. Is someone else well known for it?
Social handles:
check that the name, or something close, is free on the platforms you'll use.
Domain:
check that a web address is free (next step).
If a name fails any check, move to the next one on your list. Ask an accountant or lawyer if you're unsure.
Step 3: Buy your domain
Your domain is your web address. Choose
.ca
if your customers are mostly Canadian (you need a Canadian connection to register one) or
.com
if they're everywhere; buy both if you can. A domain usually costs about $15 to $30 a year. You can buy it from a registrar such as GoDaddy, or through your website builder (next lesson).

At checkout, registrars offer many add-ons. You usually only need the domain itself and privacy protection (which hides your home address from public records; it's often free). Turn on auto-renew, so you never lose it by accident.
Step 4: Grow your brand sheet into a brand kit
Add to the brand sheet from Lesson S5:
Your name, tagline and one-sentence description
Your logo in a few versions (full colour, one colour, and small for social profiles)
Your voice: three words for how you sound, and a few words you'd never use
Photos of you working, not only your profile photo

If you plan to trademark your logo, remember from Lesson S5: Canva's own help page says logos made from its templates or stock graphics can't be registered. Use your name in a font, simple shapes you draw yourself, or a designer.
Example (not a real member):

Diane, a retired HR director, wanted to call her coaching business "Second Wind." The registry and Google showed dozens of businesses with that name. She chose "Diane Moore Coaching", bought dianemoorecoaching.ca and .com, and used "Second Wind" as the name of her signature program instead.
Your action step:
Shortlist three names, check each one, choose, buy your domain (with auto-renew on), register your business name if you need to, and update your brand kit.

A website is your shop window, your business card and your most trusted salesperson, open all night. It doesn't need to be big. Five clear pages that tell the right person what you do and how to start are worth more than twenty pretty ones. Today you'll choose your builder and get those five pages live.
Step 1: Choose your website builder
Wix:
easy drag-and-drop, lots of templates, a free plan to build and practise on. You need a paid plan to use your own domain and remove Wix's ads. We use Wix ourselves.
Systeme.io:
website, sales pages, email list, checkout and courses in one tool, with a free plan. Best if you want fewer tools to manage. We use it too.
Squarespace:
polished designs, no free plan (there's a free trial). Popular with service businesses and creatives.
Shopify:
choose it if you'll mainly sell physical products.
If you can't decide, ask yourself: will I mostly sell services and programs (Wix, Systeme.io or Squarespace) or products (Shopify)? And do I want everything in one place (Systeme.io)?
Step 2: The five pages
Home:
in one sentence at the top, who you help and how. Then the problem, what you offer, a few words of proof, and one main button ("Book a call" or "See the program").
About:
your story, why you do this, and a good photo. Make it about how your story helps
them
Work With Me (or Shop):
your offers, what's included, who they're for, the price or "from" price, and a button for each.
Free Gift:
your email sign-up page (Lesson D3).
Contact:
a simple form or your business email, and where you're based.
Also add a short
privacy policy
page. If you collect names and emails, you need to tell people what you do with them. Your website builder or email tool usually offers a template; adapt it, and ask a professional if you're unsure.
Step 3: Connect your domain and email

Connect the domain you bought in Lesson D1 (your builder has step-by-step instructions). For an email address at your own domain, such as diane@dianemoorecoaching.ca, Google Workspace is a common choice, with a monthly fee per person. Some builders include email too.
Step 4: Check it like a stranger

Most people will see your site on a phone. Check every page on yours. Then ask two friends to look for 30 seconds and tell you what you do and what they'd click. If they can't, simplify the top of your home page. Use large, readable text and strong contrast; your audience will thank you.
Example (not a real member):

Diane built her site on Wix in two weekends. Her home page opens with "I help women in their 50s and 60s find work they love after a career change," and one button: "Book a free 20-minute chat." Her first two clients came from people her friends sent to the site.
Your action step:
Choose your builder, build the five pages plus a privacy policy, connect your domain, and test it on your phone and with two friends.

t4.name: Email That Works While You Sleep

content.text: Most people who visit your website aren't ready to buy today. If they leave, you'll probably never see them again. If they join your email list, you can build trust over weeks and be the first person they think of when they're ready. Today you'll set up a sign-up gift, a welcome series that runs on its own, and a simple monthly newsletter.
Step 1: Choose your email tool
MailerLite:
our pick, and what we use. Free for up to 500 subscribers and 12,000 emails a month, with sign-up forms, landing pages and automations.
Systeme.io:
if you built your website there, its email is built in.
Kit:
popular with creators, with a free plan.
ScoreApp:
if a quiz suits your business, for example "What's your next-career personality?" It's a paid tool, and many businesses find a quiz brings more sign-ups than a PDF.
Step 2: Your sign-up gift

One small, quick win for your ideal client: a checklist, a short guide, a quiz, or a short video. It should solve one problem in 10 to 15 minutes and lead naturally toward what you sell. Put the sign-up on your Free Gift page and your home page.
Step 3: Your welcome series (five emails)
Set these to send automatically, one every two or three days after someone signs up:
Here's your gift:
a warm welcome, the gift, and one question to reply to.
My story:
why you do this work, and what you understand about their situation.
A quick win:
your single most useful tip.
What changed for someone:
a client story (with permission) or your own before-and-after.
An invitation:
your offer, who it's for, and how to start. A free call or a first step is fine.
Write them like letters to one person. Short paragraphs, your own voice, one link per email. An AI tool can help you draft (see the AI lesson), but the stories must be yours.
Step 4: Your monthly newsletter

Once a month, send one email to everyone with three things: one helpful thing, one personal thing, and one invitation (your offer, a class or an event). Put it on your calendar after your monthly money date.
Step 5: Follow the rules
As in Track 1, Lesson A4: only email people who signed up, include your mailing address (a P.O. box is fine) and an unsubscribe link. Canada's anti-spam law (CASL) and the US CAN-SPAM Act require it.
Example (not a real member):

Diane's gift is a quiz: "Which of the five career paths suits your next chapter?" Her fifth welcome email invites people to a free 20-minute chat. About one in fifteen people who finish the welcome series book a chat.
Your action step:
Set up your email tool, create your gift and sign-up form, write and switch on your five welcome emails, and schedule your first newsletter.

A bigger business usually means selling more than one-hour sessions: a package, a group program, a course or a paid community. Done well, they help more people and earn more for your time. Today you'll choose the format for your first program and set up the tools to sell and deliver it.
Step 1: Choose your format
One-to-one package:

for example, six sessions over three months. The easiest to start, and the most personal. Tools: a booking link, video calls and a payment link (as in Track 1, Lesson A5), plus a shared folder for each client.
Group program:
a small group meets live, say weekly for six weeks. You earn more per hour and members help each other. Tools: video calls, a payment link, and a place to share recordings and talk between calls.
Online course:
recorded lessons people work through on their own. Takes longest to make, but can sell for years. Best built
after
you've taught the material live a few times.
Paid community or membership:
a monthly fee for ongoing support, content and connection. Works once you have an audience who wants to stay with you.
Our advice:
start with a one-to-one package or a small live group. Run it with three to five people at a founding price. You'll learn what people really need before you build a course.
Step 2: Choose where it lives
Systeme.io:
sales page, checkout, course area and email in one, with a free plan and no transaction fees beyond card processing. Our pick for most women starting out. We use it ourselves.
Skool:
a simple combined community and course. $9 a month with 10% of each sale, or $99 a month with 2.9%. The cheaper plan costs less until you're earning about $1,250 a month from it.
Circle:
more flexible and polished, for when you have a larger community or several programs. It's what SWC runs on.
Payhip:
a simple, low-cost way to sell a course or downloads.
Whichever you choose, payments usually run through Stripe (Lesson S3).
Step 3: Write the program down
Name, who it's for and the result
What's included: number of sessions, length, materials, support between sessions
Price, payment options, and your refund policy (write it down before anyone pays)
Start date and schedule
Step 4: Plan the welcome

The first 48 hours after someone pays shape how they feel about the whole program. Set up a welcome email that goes out automatically with what happens next, the dates, how to join calls and where to find materials. Then send a personal note too.
Example (not a real member):

Diane ran "Second Wind", a six-week group program for five women, at a founding price of $297. Their questions became the outline for her course a year later. She runs the group on Skool, with weekly Zoom calls.
Your action step:
Choose your format and platform, write your program down, set up the sales page and checkout, and write your welcome email. Then invite your first three to five people.

When you have five clients, you can keep it all in your head. At twenty, things start slipping: a follow-up forgotten, an invoice not sent, a file you can't find. Systems aren't about being corporate. They're about never dropping a ball, so you can enjoy the work. Today you'll set up four simple systems and one automation.
System 1: A client tracker

One place that shows everyone you're working with, or talking to, and what happens next. For each person: name, email, how they found you, what they bought, the stage they're at (enquiry, booked, active, finished), and the next step with a date.
A spreadsheet:
fine for up to about 20 people.
Airtable (free plan):
a friendlier, more powerful spreadsheet. We run SWC on it.
Trello (free plan):
cards you drag across columns, good if you think visually.
System 2: Templates you reuse
Write these once and save them in your "My Business" folder:
Client agreement:
what you'll provide, the price, payment terms, your cancellation and refund policy, and confidentiality. Have a lawyer look at your first version if your work is high-stakes.
Invoice:
Wave's free plan sends professional invoices and tracks who has paid.
Emails you send often:
welcome, session reminder, follow-up, thank you and "how did it go?"
System 3: Your calendar

Put your working hours from your Launch Plan into your calendar as blocks: client time, making or creating time, admin time and your monthly money date. Then guard them. Google Calendar comes free with your Gmail.
System 4: One automation
An automation is a small robot that does a repetitive job for you.
Zapier

connects your tools and has a free plan for simple automations. For example: when someone pays through Stripe, Zapier adds them to your client tracker in Airtable and tags them in MailerLite so they get your welcome email. Choose the one repetitive task that takes you the most time each week and automate just that one. We use Zapier for SWC.
Write it down as you go
Every time you do something more than twice, write the steps in a document: "How I onboard a new client." These become your routines, and they're what lets you get help later (Lesson D7).
Example (not a real member):

Diane's tracker lives in Airtable. When a client pays, a Zapier automation adds her to the tracker and to MailerLite. Diane used to spend about an hour a week on this. Now she spends five minutes checking it worked.
Your action step:
Set up your client tracker, write your agreement and email templates, block your calendar, and build one automation.

AI tools can save you hours on the writing every business needs: posts, emails, product descriptions, page copy. Think of AI as a keen assistant who types fast and has read a lot, but has never met your customers and sometimes makes things up. You stay the boss: your experience, your facts and your voice. Today you'll set up an AI assistant and use it for three real tasks.
Tools worth knowing
ChatGPT
and
Claude:
general assistants for writing, planning and thinking things through. Both have free plans.
Holo:
makes on-brand social posts, ads and emails once you've given it your brand. A paid tool, worth it once you're posting a lot. We use it.
DeeVid:
turns text or a photo into a short video. Useful for social media once you're comfortable with the basics. We use it too.
Start with one general assistant. Add the others only if you find yourself needing them.
The recipe for a good request
AI gives generic answers to generic requests. Tell it:
Who you are:
"I'm a retired HR director who coaches women in their 50s and 60s through career changes."
Who it's for:
"My readers are women who've been laid off or retired early and feel lost."
What you want:
"Write five ideas for Facebook posts about..."
How it should sound:
"Warm, plain, no jargon, like a friend over coffee." Paste in something you've written so it can copy your voice.
Length and format:
"Under 100 words each."
Then push back: "Make it shorter," "Less salesy," "Give me three more options."
Good jobs for AI
First drafts of posts, emails and product descriptions
Turning your rough notes into a clear outline
Ten ideas when you're stuck
Making your writing shorter and clearer
Explaining a confusing setting or term in plain words
Never hand it these
Facts and figures you haven't checked:
AI can invent statistics, prices and rules that sound true. Check anything important.
Testimonials or reviews:
never let AI write a customer's words. Use only real ones, with permission.
Private client information:
don't paste names, health details or anything personal about clients into an AI tool.
Legal, tax or medical decisions:
AI can explain; a professional decides.
Your stories:
AI can tidy them, but they must be true and yours. That's what people buy.
Example (not a real member):

Diane pastes her rough notes from a client call (with no names) into Claude and asks for a short, warm Facebook post in her voice. She edits two sentences, adds a detail only she would know, and posts it. What used to take her an hour now takes fifteen minutes.
Your action step:
Set up one AI assistant, write a short paragraph about you, your customers and your voice that you can paste in each time, and use it for three real tasks this week.

t4.name: When and How to Get Help

content.text: You can't build something bigger by doing every single job yourself forever. At some point, the best use of your time is the work only you can do, and paying someone else for the rest. Today you'll work out when that point comes, and get ready for your first helper, even if you don't hire yet.
When is it time?
Go back to your hand-off column from Lesson 10 ("Do It, Learn It or Hand It Off"). A task is ready to hand off when:
It takes you several hours a month, and
Someone else could do it well with clear instructions, and
Those hours, spent on clients or selling, would earn more than the helper costs.
For example: if bookkeeping takes you four hours a month and you earn $60 an hour with clients, those hours are worth $240 to you. A bookkeeper at $40 an hour who does it in two hours costs $80.
Who helps with what
Virtual assistant (VA):
email, scheduling, posting, simple admin. Works remotely, usually paid by the hour.
Bookkeeper:
records your money each month and gets things ready for your accountant. Many prefer you to use QuickBooks.
Designer:
your logo (if you want to trademark it), graphics, a more polished website.
Tech helper:
setting up your website, email or automations.

Most women start with a few hours a month of help from a VA or bookkeeper, as a contractor rather than an employee. The rules about who counts as a contractor differ by country, so ask your accountant before you hire.
Get ready: write the routine

Nobody can help you if the job only lives in your head. For the first task you'll hand off, write the routine: the steps in order, the logins needed, what "done" looks like and when it's due. Even better, record yourself doing it.
Loom
records your screen and voice, and its free plan is fine for short videos.
Hire carefully
Ask other business owners for recommendations first (The Lounge is a great place).
Pay for a small trial task before you commit to more.
Share access safely: use your password manager's sharing feature or add them as a user, never by emailing passwords. Remove their access when the work ends.
Agree in writing on the task, the rate, the hours and confidentiality.
Example (not a real member):

Diane's first helper was a VA for six hours a month, posting to social media and sending her newsletter. She recorded three Loom videos to show how. The VA costs Diane less than one coaching session a month, and gives her back a full day.
Your action step:
Choose the first task you'll hand off (now or later), work out what it's worth, write the routine and record a Loom video of it. Then fill in your My System checklist.

t4.name: Photos That Sell, Taken on Your Phone

content.text: A bonus lesson open to every track.
Online, your photo
is

your product. People can't touch it, try it on or turn it over, so the photo has to do all of that for them. The good news: the phone in your pocket is enough. Light and background matter far more than the camera.
1. Find the light

Set up next to a large window during the day, with the window to one side of your item. Turn off the room lights; mixing daylight and lamp light makes colours look odd. If the sun is harsh, tape a sheet of baking paper or a thin white curtain over the window to soften it. A piece of white card on the other side bounces light back into the shadows.
2. Keep the background simple

A plain white or light background (a sheet of poster board curved up a wall works beautifully), or a simple natural surface that suits your brand: wood, linen, slate. The item should be the star. Clear the clutter.
3. Take the set
For each product:
The hero shot:
the whole item, straight on, filling most of the frame. This becomes your main photo.
Other angles:
side, back, top.
The close-up:
the detail that shows quality: stitching, texture, a brush stroke.
Size:
in someone's hands, on a table setting, or beside an everyday object.
In use:
worn, displayed or being used, so people can picture it in their own home.
Any flaws:
for resale especially, honest photos of marks or wear prevent returns.
4. Phone tips
Wipe your lens first. It's almost always smudgy.
Tap the screen on your item to focus, then slide the brightness slightly up or down.
Don't zoom in; move closer instead.
Hold the phone level with the item, not looking down from above (unless it's a flat-lay).
Turn off the flash.
5. A light touch afterwards

In your phone's photo editor, straighten, crop and brighten a little. Keep colours true; a buyer who gets something that looks different will be disappointed. Canva can resize photos for each platform, and its paid Pro plan can remove backgrounds.
For photos of you
The same rules apply: face the window, phone at your eye level, plain background. Take twenty and choose the best (see Lesson S5).
Your action step:
Set up your window "studio", photograph one product (or yourself) using the full set, and replace your weakest photo online.
